Surely it is not too much to ask Chinese children, who go to China intending to return to Canada, to substantiate their identity before they go, so that possibility of evasion when they return might be made less easy.
Paragraph (c) of clause 5 is the one that deals with merchants and students. That has been badly printed. By a mistake in the way it is printed, the intention is mateiially changed. The word "degrees" at the top of page 4 should be the end of a line, and then it should begin "who shall," in such a way that the words "who shall substantiate" would apply to both merchants and students. As it reads now, it gives the impression, which I have heard repeatedly commented upon, that the word "merchant" in subclause (1) has absolutely no restriction on it whatever, and that is the meaning of it as the paragraph is now printed. It goes on to say "students. . who shall substantiate" but for lack of precision in printing and its being printed in the way that I have mentioned, a wrong impression is given-it is really intended to say that both classes, merchants and students, shall substantiate their status. The way the paragraph is printed, it applies only to the one word "student," and this has given rise to the impression that the merchant is going to have a very wide-open door.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that it was decided to determine who should be considered as merchants or students before they left China, and the drift of his remarks was that their status would be ascertained, if not decided, in China. As regards that clause, I was glad to hear that explanation; but the clause says only that the passports shall be endorsed or vised by a Canadian immigration officer at the place where the Chinamen leave. But it also says that the final decision shall be at the port of entry, because there the Chinamen shall substantiate their status to the satisfaction i>f the controller, subject to the approval of the minister. We have there a sort of dual control. Certainly it would appear to me that the first officer in China had little or nothing to do except to put his imprimatur on the passport. If it was intended that he should be the deciding official, his powers in that regard should be better defined. As two men are involved, this matter of putting the vise on the passport will drift into a mere formality. He will do what is formally known as vise-ing a passport; he will simply put his name on it. I think the bill could be improved a great deal in that respect.
Chinese Immigration

As regards students the clause says that students coming to Canada properly endorsed, and so on, shall be allowed in free. The provision should be made not only to ensure that they continue to be students while in Canada, but that they leave Canada at the end of their period of education. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mc-Quarrie) pointed out, there was a case quite recently where a student, not lopg after coming into Canada turned out to be labouring in a mill. Under conditions as outlined, there is no real check.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Under clause 27, the moment a man ceases to belong to any of the exempt classes, he is liable to deportation.

He is liable under clause 27 to be picked up in the street if he is found to be in Canada without any right, so to speak. But who is to find him and who is to pick him up? I would make this suggestion: Supposing 200 students come into Canada and they enter a college for a fixed period. If they are really genuinely going to be educated, the Chinese comptroller in Vancouver should have knowledge of those boys, of where they are and to what schools they are going. He could once a year or so check the records of the school or university in order to find out if they are still students. Let him keep in touch with the schools or universities and if so many graduate say this year, he will expect to see so many educated Chinese boys leave the country. The way the situation is at present, they come in and as my hon. friend for New Westminster says, they drift away, they sneak away, and if they do put in a perfunctory education for a few months, they leave then.' There is no possible means under clause 27 of keeping in touch with these students. A Chinaman may get into court for some offence and you can ask him where his papers are and so on; but it would be more satisfactory, easier and cheaper, to check him up in the college from time to time than to chase him all over the province, in the hope of finding him in some odd corner.
The definition of "merchant" should have been in clause 2, amongst the other definitions. I can not say that I altogether agree with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster. I think it is desirable that we should encourage our trade with the orient. We all admit that and I do not think the suggestion of the hon. member for New Westminster quite covers that, because he restricts the definition to a man act-
TMr. Neill.]
ing practically as a commision agent. There would be no objection to a man acting as a wholesaler of Chinese or oriental imports in Canada, provided that there was no evasion.
I think the regulations mentioned by the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) this afternoon, although I could not get him to read them the second time and I only heard them read once, seemed to be quite appropriate and sufficient to check fraudulent entry of merchants. He should, however, put that regulation, which he says is in existence, into the bill, and it would meet the whole situation. The worst of a regulation is this: that it is liable to be abrogated at the whim of one man. This minister might be all right; but the next one might not, or his deputy might not and it is not wise to have the whole substance of a piece of legislation depend upon the whim of one man in the department. If the definition is sufficient to effect the purpose aimed at, and it can be put in a regulation, surely it can be put into the bill, and in that case there will be no trouble about the matter. I would also suggest that the number entering in one year should be restricted by joint agreement, so that not more than so many shall be allowed to enter in any one year.
The minister might well consider the idea of holding over this clause until the next time the bill comes down and having printed his amendment and that of the hon. member for New Westminster so that we could study them to better advantage. There are several other small things in this bill that need re-adjustment, but we can deal with them as we come to them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With most of the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Neill), I for one agree. He clearly draws a distinction between an evasion of the law through the endeavour of some Chinese coming into the country to act in a fraudulent manner, and an effort on the part of the administration to permit those who, in the interest of the country, should be allowed to come in, to enter in a way which will be thoroughly honourable and in accordance with recognized procedure. The various communications that have been read have, for the most part, come from Retail Merchants' Associations, and evidently it is the retailers who are afraid of Chinese competition in their trade. If that is the case, might I suggest to my hon. friends from British Columbia that, perhaps, if the word "merchant" were changed to read "merchants engaged in import and export trade," that would remove any of the serious or justifiable alarm which retail merchants have

Chinese Immigration
and at the same time permit international trade of a character which it is eminently desirable to foster between the two countries? I would not object to the greater part of the amendment my hon. friend has suggested, were he to couple it with the words I have used, so that the section would read:
Merchants engaged in import and export trade, including sales agents and purchasing agents while representing bona fide Chinese exporters and importers carrying on international trade between Canada and China, buying from or selling to persons, firms or corporations in Canada.
If these two sentences were incorporated in the act they would pretty effectively cover what the committee is aiming at and at the same time they would not be invidious in any way to persons who might be sensitive on matters of this kind. In proposing this I would draw the attention of the committee to the last part of section 3 which has not yet been enacted but which will undoubtedly pass substantially as it is later on. It gives to the Governor in Council, in other words, the minister, power to make regulations providing for the payment of fees for the furnishing of substantial certificates, endorsing passports, "and other administrative work in connection with the carrying out of this act." Under that power the minister, with this definition of merchant before him, would be in a position to supplement the definition by whatever regulations appear to be demanded by the necessities of the case. My hon. friend in referring to the students has mentioned the desirability of keeping track of this class of immigrants as they come into the country. I can hardly imagine a minister who would not make regulations which would contemplate that course being followed. I believe however that it is preferable to leave to the minister the making of such regulations rather than to have the act itself declare that every Chinese student, regardless of who he may be or of the home from which he comes should be kept track of from day to day and year by year, by some system of registration, from the moment he comes to the country to the moment he leaves it. I think that regulation can effect all that is necessary in this regard. If this broader definition would meet the situation, the government would be agreeable to incorporating the words I have cited in the act itself. I hope that this meets with my hon. friend's approval.
Would not the Prime Minister and the Acting Minister of Immigration be willing to leave this matter over as suggested by the member for Comox-Al-berni so that we might study the proposed amendment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I merely
wished to present it to the committee with that end in view. I think it would be well to leave it over and proceed to the other sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen have any suggestions to make regarding students I should be glad to have them now, because if I have any amendments to make I desire to have all the views of hon. members before me.

I would call the attention of the minister to the last three or four lines of the section which refers to a passport:
Issued in and by the government of China and endorsed by a Canadian immigration officer.
If I am correctly informed, the government of China with headquarters at Peking is not functioning in the Canton district from which practically all immigrants to Canada come. There is a de facto government at Canton, a rebel government one might call it, I suppose, which controls the district, a very large area comprising two or three of the southern provinces; and I understand that the Peking government is not in control of that part of the country at all. Under these circumstances how could you get the endorsation of the Chinese government in respect of matters affecting immigrants from Canton?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, the act is looking more or less to stable government in China. The first provision is that the passport shall be issued by the government; that is the first requirement that the student must comply with. I doubt myself that this would be practicable at the moment, with existing difficulties in China. As a matter of fact there are two governments there at the moment, and I presume that either government issuing a passport would have to be recognized.

I am afraid my hon. friend would find himself in .serious difficulty. How can the Canadian government recognise a government which is at enmity with that government which is represented by the Consul-General from China in this country? The Consul-General with whom my hon. friend has been negotiating is the representative of the government that has its headquarters at Peking; and if my hon. friend were to recognize passports issued by the so-called rebel government of the south, from which district alone practically this immigration comes, I anticipate trouble. Frankly, I really apprehend serious difficulty when my hon. friend comes to place his officer over
Chinese Immigration

there. We had a great deal of difficulty in years gone by and I am very sceptical about the success of this movement with an officer of the Canadian government in that country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
share my hon. friend's apprehension concerning these difficulties. I think he will notice that the final test in this case, as indeed it is with regard to all other nationals entering Canada, is at the port of Vancouver. That is where the final disposition of any national of China will take place; and as a matter of fact the port of landing in this country is the place of final disposition of the national of any other country coming to Canada. At the moment the British government is doing business with China and passports are being issued by that government that are recognised so far as China is concerned. I admit, of course, that there is a serious difficulty, but the act is looking to a settled condition of affairs in China. If conditions do not become settled there the result may be that we shall receive few people from that country, which I suppose would satisfy my hon. friend.

Yes, absolutely. But this act is intended to repeal the present statute which does away with the $500 head tax, and there is a danger that in the hiatus between now and the time when there are settled conditions in China the courts may declare that it is possible for those immigrants to come in. We know from experience that unless legislation is very carefully drawn, applications will be made to the courts and my hon. friend's hands will be tied, as his predecessors' have been time and again. At the present moment the minister finds it impossible to deport some couple of hundreds of people convicted under the Drug Act, and this through no fault of his particularly-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We had
nothing to do with it.

-but because of the fact that the act has been so interpreted by the courts as to prevent the minister's acting. That is what I am afraid of here. I fear that the minister may find himself faced with a difficulty of that kind, and we might have thousands of Chinese landed here and experience another riot such as occurred in 1908.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provisions of the act are being very much restricted; they apply practically to two classes of citizens of China.

I quite understand all that. I am merely calling attention to this matter
fMr. Stevens.]
and if .the minister is satisfied I want to tell him that I am not, and we will cry quits so far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend know that the existing act is not repealed until this act comes into force? The moment this act comes into force the class of Chinese admitted to come in under the head tax will be excluded. So that the hiatus my hon. friend talks about is a pure figment of the imagination.
I hope it is, but probably I shall have the pleasure of recalling this conversation to the attention of the government at some future date.

Mr. Chairman, I have not very much to add to what has already been said on this subject. A number of telegrams have been read with respect to Chinese immigration; I have four along the same lines, but I shall refrain from putting them on Hansard. Expression has been given here to the opinion that it is quite satisfactory to the people of British Columbia to allow the entry of Chinese students. Well, I cannot see the matter in that light. Why should British Columbia educate the people of the Orient? Why cannot the orientals build schools in their own countries and get European teachers to come out and teach them English and French if they want to learn those languages? These orientals make very strong objections unless their children are allowed to be educated in our schools and colleges with our own boys and girls. I do not think it is right that oriental students should be allowed to mix with our young people. In Victoria last summer the orientals refused pointblank to be segregated from Canadian school children. To give the committee some idea of what the people of the East think on this question I will read a few extracts translated from an article which was published in an oriental paper. It stated:
There is danger ahead. Discrimination has been shown in the school question and in the fishing question. This question is a life and death struggle to us Japanese, and we should determine our objective.
This is rather strong languege from people who come into our country although they know we do not want them here. The orientals must know that they are not wanted in British Columbia. And what is their object in coming into this country if they are putting up a "life and death struggle" as they call it? In my opinion their object is to get control of the Pacific coast, including all British Columbia.

Chinese Immigration
I do not think orientals should be allowed into this country under any conditions. We do not have to bring people into our own houses simply because we do business with them and there is no reason why these orientals should come here and occupy our country simply because they want to do business with us. I see the South African authorities are talking of giving the orientals there a bonus to return home. I think this government could well afford to give back to every Chinaman here what we got from him-the $500 he paid to enter the Dominion-on condition he would leave, and thus rid the country of a whole lot of Chinamen and do ourselves a good turn.
In South Africa the people are talking of segregating the Chinese; that may have to be done yet in British Columbia, for the two races should not be brought together. It seems to me that if the good Lord had intended orientals and white people to live in the same country he would not have put the Pacific ocean between them. I think the people of the East should remain in their owe countries. I do not see why we should admit them here and educate them in our own schools and colleges. I could cite a number of cases where the mingling of oriental children with our children in British Columbia has been a great detriment to the latter. The eastern ideals of morality and citizenship are entirely different to ours, and I do not see why our children's ideals should be lowered by their contact with the children of orientals. In China and Japan the men can have as many wives as they want, and there is no question but that this and similar views are drilled into our children where they are educated with the children of orientals. We do not want such ideas to be propagated here. Therefore I take very strong exception to allowing oriental students to come into this country to be educated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to remove a misapprehension under which my hon friend is apparently labouring. He seems to think that it is the intention to have such students educated in British Columbia. As a matter of fact the clause in the bill relating to students has reference to universities conferring degrees. Undoubtedly if any university hesitates to take Chinese students they will not be admitted there. For instance, if the University of British Columbia thinks well not to admit Chinese students, why certainly these students will not go to that university. But Toronto, Kingston
and Montreal universities are willing and anxious to take Chinese students. It seems . to me it would be a mistake on the part of our people if we prevented educated young men and women from China getting the benefits of higher education here and then returning home to do what they can to acquaint the Orient with what my hon. friend has spoken of as the higher standards of living on this continent. I think we ought to be prepared, if we have it, to spread the light of our civilization in the Orient, and so far as I can see it our universities afford one of the best means to that end.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-At Vancouver and Victoria only, with sdveral exceptions:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the idea of this?
What is the idea of specifying Vancouver and Victoria?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are
the principal ports at which most of the nationals of China will make application for entry. It is the intention of the government to keep a staff of officials at these ports to conduct proper examinations. It would be a very expensive proposition, for example, if we had to keep similar staffs at St. John, Halifax, Quebec and other ports.

We would be delighted
if the minister would substitute St. John and Halifax for Vancouver and Victoria-or what might be better still, Montreal and Toronto.
If that suggestion is acceptable to the minister I shall be very glad indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it will be admitted that the two ports mentioned are the natural ports through which most of the nationals of China do enter Canada.

It is my opinion that if the government would incorporate in this bill one or two of the eastern ports the people of British Columbia would take it upon themselves to exclude the Chinese from entering their province from the east.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-Prohibited classes:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the need of such prolixity in this clause? Are not these classes just the same as those prohibited from all countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.

Chinese Immigration

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Why does not the clause simply read:
Classes prohibited under section so-and-so of the
Immigration Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not being a lawyer I cannot answer my hon. friend, except to say that you have within the bounds of the one act all the prohibited classes named without having to refer to the general Immigration Act.

There are no exemptions
from the regular act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It seems to me the better method of legislation would be to have one immigration act and then have, if there is going to be a distinction between China and other countries, parts applicable to
9 p.m. China or to any other country as to which special legislation applies. It would be a much more compact and comprehensive way of getting legislation on our books.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To some extent I agree with my hon. friend, but he will notice there are provisions under the Chinese Immigration Act which do not appear in the other act. I can see no other reason for going to the trouble of inserting the prohibited classes of the general act, except that it saves the trouble of consulting the latter act in so far as Chinese immigration is concerned. It will also be noted that practically all the clauses of this bill apply peculiarly to Chinese immigration, and to it alone.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the government contemplate further legislation on Japanese immigration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not further legislation at present, but I will have an announcement to make later with regard to Japanese immigration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will there be further legislation following that announcement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I might perhaps state to my right hon. friend that as I mentioned here some little time ago, negotiations have been carried on between this government and the Japanese government, and as a result of those negotiations the Japanese government themselves have offered to place a greater restriction on the classes of labour coming to Canada than has hitherto existed. They have expressed the hope that it will not be found necessary for the parliament of Canada to legislate in a manner which might ere-
ate serious embarrassment to the government of Japan in Japan itself and they would hope that such restriction as they are prepared to place on the classes of labour to which we object will in the eyes of our government prove sufficient to prevent the necessity of introducing any invidious legislation. The government is prepared, at least for a time, to give the Japanese government the opportunity of revealing its intentions and good faith in this matter. If it should appear from the figures themselves, which probably will prove more eloquent than any words, that the restriction which the Japanese government itself is contemplating is not sufficient to meet the needs of the situation, then legislation may be necessary at a later stage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not very familiar with the legislative history of the matter. Is there special Japanese immigration legislation now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Japanese just come in under the general Immigration Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is an agreement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Subject to the mysterious agreement. Perhaps while I am on my feet I might make a few remarks as to the general principles that I think should underlie this character of legislation-in fact, the one principle; I do not think there is more than one. There has been some discussion as to how far we should go and how far we ought not to go in' restricting immigration. It has not been carried on with a view to making any contrast of party history except on the part of the hon. member for Comox-Allberni (Mr. Neill) and there is no need for such contrast at all. There have been progressive restrictions all through the last three score years. The last restrictive enactment on Chinese immigration was in the year 1921, when substantial effective restrictions were put on, not effective enough I know. There were other restrictions in 1917. These were under the late government.
Now I want to lay down this principle which I think is sound, which I think other countries have followed, and which our country must follow; that we should determine our immigration law not out of animosity to any country or to any race, not out of prejudice to any country or to any race, nor on the other hand out of a fear of the sensitiveness of any country or of any race, but solely out of consideration for our own internal domestic

Chinese Immigration
necessities. We have done that; we have done it all along, and we ought to continue to do it. Other countries have done it. Other countries have gone much farther than we.
How could it be said, for example, that in the legislation we have here consideration is shown for the sensibilities of China, that we have taken care not to offend the Chinese Empire, that there is no invidious distinction? Why, the whole bill is invidious, if you can have anything invidious in immigration legislation. I do not complain of it on that account. As long as the bill is founded on the just needs of our country from its domestic internal standpoint that is all that is required. But to argue that a bill excluding merchants would offend China but that this bill is all right and will not offend China, because under it merchants are admitted though it keeps out farmers, labourers, clerks, salesmen, professional men, laundrymen, all sorts and conditions of men, seems to me to verge on nonsense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think that can be said.

Well, if there is any
offence in the world the offence comes from distinctions between China and any other country. But we have to do it, and we have to do it on the basis of our own needs, and if it meets our own needs better to keep merchants out. then we ought to do it, and China would have no just cause of offence. China has an equal right so far as we are concerned to do the same thing. I believe-I will not say I believe, but I would not be very much surprised if in the course of time public opinion which is built upon and which grows out of public necessities, will demand more and more restrictions than any that are called for by hon. gentlemen behind me. It does not so demand to-day. Public opinion to-day is prepared in view of other things to be gained thereby to admit students, to admit trade representatives; not merchants, but trade representatives, for the sake as respects the first of making Canadian learning known throughout the world, for the sake as respects the second of developing the trade of our country. If other considerations later on weigh more heavily than those, two, then public opinion will demand the exclusion of both. But the reason we exclude now until we get right up to trade representatives and up to students is simply because we have to do so for our protection in this country. That is the only principle that really governs us, and do not let us pretend that any other
does; I do not think any other ever has. Just as soon as you select a country or a race and you place around it barriers and restraints that you do not apply to immigration in general, then as respects that country or race there is something invidious. But because it does exist it does not mean that it arises out of any feeling of unfriendliness, any feeling of international animosity or anything of that kind. It arises out of conditions peculiar to ourselves which we have to take care of in the interests of ourselves and of the world. I hope I have made myself clear.
I would define "merchant" if I were the minister. I am glad the government has consented at last to do so. It is simply foolish to argue that the Chinese are quite satisfied if merchants are defined by regulation, but that they would be offended if they are defined in the bill. We cannot stand on a foundation of that sort. I would define "merchant" if I were the minister, and I would define it most specifically so that there can be no dispute, for I say this to the minister: You are going to find your representative in China clothed with remarkable, extensive and very perilous powers, very perilous powers indeed, and you may find yourself in serious trouble for that reason. Do not have those powers any wider than you can possibly avoid. Let this parliament speak as to what a merchant should be. It really is intended to be defined for according to the statement of the minister himself, according to the proposal the Prime Minister later suggested to the committee,. what is really intended is, not a merchant but a trade representative, a merchant, if you may so describe him, in the international sense as between two countries and two alone, China and Canada. Consequently I would define "merchant," and I would have some other definitions that we will arrive at before we reach the end of the bill. It would have been better if we had not passed clause 2 because it is clause 2 that will need to be amended. There must be something left to regulation, I admit, but the minimum should always be left, and if ever there was a bill where the least should be left to regulation it is such a bill as this.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-Minister may authorize admission for specified period:

I think I correctly interpret the minister's intention when I say that the purpose of this clause is to reserve a right to admit persons under special reques* such as, clergy or the wives of some merchants, and
Chinese Immigration

so forth, who may be excluded by the provisions of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think it is the intention of clause 9 to permit the permanent admission of any persons.

I was just coming to that. I would like, however, to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that this clause does permit of the admission of indentured labour. Now it does not so state, and it may not be in his mind to do so, but the clause as it stands would permit the entry of indentured labour. I am looking forward and this clause, perhaps, is one that will not be invoked very frequently and may become, for the time being a dead letter; but at some time, under pressure of some, perhaps by reason of ordinary circumstances, an application may bfe made to the Minister of Immigration who may be tempted to admit some indentured labour under this clause. To that I am most bitterly opposed; I do not believe in indentured labour under any circumstance. We had the experience many years ago of Chinese indentured labour and we want no repetition of that experience. Does the minister really consider this clause necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would like to say to my hon. friend that I have steadily stood out against representations made to widen the classes of people who would be admissible under clause 5-that is merchants and students virtually and the diplomatic corps; but there is one contention, and there seems to be good reason for it, that missionaries and teachers of Chinese origin might very well be admitted. Thelefore, I think, under clause 9, for a restricted period, the minister might have that authority. Then again there is the case of tourists who wish to come and visit the country; they might be admitted under a permit. If my hon. friend sees an opportunity, at some future time, for some corporation, perhaps, to come to the minister and say "We want 100, or 150, or [DOT] 200 labourers temporarily" that might be provided for in the bill if it is thought the power is too wide but I do think that clause 9 will be necessary and will be needed for legitimate purposes, although I may say frankly I would not for a moment consider that indentured labour should come in under its provisions.

My hon. friend will admit that it could; the power is there. I know that it is not in his mind, but we have had the witness to-day of the transfer of one minister, a very excellent gentleman, from one

department to another. My hon. friend may be Minister of Agriculture next session; we can never tell.
Minister of Justice.

No he would hardly be Minister of Justice because I do not think he has-shall I say?-the technique for that portfolio. But we might have a minister here who was prejudiced against the ideas of this bill; such a thing might possibly happen. So I would like to see that provided against, if it were possible. I am not prepared with an amendment offhand. The clause reads:
The minister may authorize the admission to Canada of any person of Chinese origin or descent without being subject to the provision of this act-
It is a very broad clause, it ought to be restricted in some manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no notion the power would be used for any other purposes than those I have named; and really the object of the clause is to avoid specifying in the bill any classes of people who might come into the country temporarily. However, it could be used for the purpose which my hon. friend has mentioned.

We might add the words:
Provided however that this section shall not apply to the admission of labourers or artisans.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Labourers are excluded as the bill stands.

No, if the Prime Minister will look at this he will realize my point. Under this clause all other provisions of the act can be ignored. Let me repeat: I am not suggesting that that is the idea in the minister's mind at the present time because I know very well it is not; but the time might come in the future when perhaps some emergency, or imagined emergency, might arise and such an application might be made to bring in 50 or 100 Chinamen, something of that character, and it would just be the opening of the way for the abuse of the very idea that forms the basis of this legislation. I frankly feel that this clause should be restricted very considerably.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Is there not in the knowledge of the strong feeling that there is on the part of the country against the admission of any number of orientals a very good guarantee that the minister will not use his powers unduly? I think that constitutes a guarantee that the minister will not go too far in the matter. Cases might come up-unforeseen cases-where it might conceivably be in the interests even of British Columbia that

Chinese Immigration
a few Chinese might be permitted to come in for some emergency purpose. I do not assume that the clause will ever be used in that way; there are, however, individual cases which come to the attention of the department -such, for example, as clergymen or tourists coming through on some special mission. I should think some latitude ought to be given to the minister to admit a few persons of that class, and it is better to give the general authority rather than to be too detailed and specific in the classes that are mentioned.
Could not that be done by order in council in specific cases?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It virtually comes to that; the minister has to give his sanction. I do not, however, think we had better add to the number of orders in council which it is necessary to pass.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister will remember, of course, that he cannot deputize this responsibility; he cannot authorize anybody else to act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are doing this purposely. We got into trouble under the general act over this matter, and I think this power should be confined to the minister. This particular case is one in which the minister should act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-Appeal to minister:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is the Immigration Act section is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is clause 11-no appeal in certain cases-the Immigration Act section also, and if it is not why is there a distinction made?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
(Reading).
There shall be no appeal from the decision of the controller, as to the rejection or deportation of any immigrant, passenger or other person found to be of Chinese origin or descent seeking to enter or land in Canada when such decision is based upon a certificate of the examining medical officer to the effect that such immigrant, passenger or other person of Chinese origin or descent is afflicted with any loathsome disease-
In that particular case it is concluded that the evidence is sufficient to bar the entry into Canada of the Chinese immigrant. I may say there has been some criticism of this from the Chinese themselves. I think it should stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do you mean that clause 11 should stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; I think the provision should remain.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-Identification and registration of Chinese immigrants.-Certificates to be delivered to immigrants permitted to land:
Does the minister propose to use the finger print identification system?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Is anything else trustworthy in the case of Asiatics?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Identification is difficult, I admit, but after considering the matter I came to the conclusion, from representations made, that it was going a bit too far, because, as my hon. friend knows, it is only used in cases of criminals.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And we do not want to have the oriental people classed as criminals.

This clause says-
And such certificate shall be prima facie evidence that the person presenting it has complied with the requirements of this act.
Now, what the minister will have to face, without question, is the system of transferring those certificates. There is no question in my mind that if a Chinaman dies, or if, as has been going on for years, he is smuggled across into the United States, or into some other country, the certificate will be passed on. We have been passing a steady stream through this country, without the knowledge of the government of Canada. They will get these certificates, will pass them on and they will be held and used, just as sure as we are sitting in this House to-night, for illegal purposes. Experience teaches us that and I think that these Chinese should be compelled to carry the certificates or an identification card on their persons.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have to carry their certificates with them.

And check up occasionally. I had a reference, which for the moment I have lost, which I wished to refer to in connection with this matter. I am very much afraid that there will be a continued evasion of this clause. Has the minister any definnite idea in mind as to how this could be prevented?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recognize the difficulty of pre-
Chinese Immigration

venting exchange of certificates, owing to the similarity of the appearance of the Chinese. If a man is in possession of a certificate, it is a most difficult thing, unless you have some other evidence, to detect fraud. We discussed the matter of taking finger prints, but afterwards dropped it. The mere fact of making the Chinaman produce the certificate on demand is not evidence that the individual holding the certificate is the one who entered under it.
There is no penalty for forgery or transfer?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes, I think there is a very severe penalty for the transference of a certificate. I quite appreciate the difficulty of proving that the man presenting the certificate is the man who really owns it.
Section 32 provides the penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One year after the act goes into force there is to be a general registration, and each individual in Canada will have to show his certificate. If he goes out of Canada, and some one comes in and uses that certificate in place of him, I confess it will be a very difficult thing to prove.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: What about the photograph?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know the photographs are there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister does not expect any of them to die. I am told they never die. Those who have British citizenship to-day are endowed with immortality. The certificate always passes to some one else who looks exactly like the original party. I fancy you will meet with that difficulty. There will be no emigration from that part of the country. All the certificates will remain, and those who died will have their counterparts in possession of the certificates.

I cannot see why there should be any objection to the finger print system. The idea in taking the finger print is that we should have some positive means of identification. We have had the experience in British Columbia in regard to naturalization papers. I have a return here, No. 187, which I got the other day, containing certain correspondence in regard to naturalization in Vancouver between the Under Secretary of State and one of the county court judges there, his honour, Judge Grant. It appeal's from that correspondence that in

some cases naturalization certificates had been granted to Japanese who had never left Japan at all. Some friend had got the naturalization papers for them.
In regard to fishing licenses, we had a great deal of trouble, and it was admitted before our British Columbia Fisheries Commission last year that there had been many cases of abuse of this kind. There were many instances of naturalization papers being transferred, for the purpose of enabling the holders for the time being to obtain fishing licenses. A photograph is of no material assistance. The photographs that will be attached to the registration certificates under the section we are considering, will be so similar that it will be almost impossible for any one to determine whether the holder for the time being of the certificate is the person who is legally entitled to that certificate or not. I cannot for the life of me see why there should be any greater indignity to a man by requiring him to allow records to be taken of his finger prints than by requiring his photograph. I think where there is this method of obtaining positive proof of identity, it should be made use of. Certainly the finger print system seems to be one that no person, not even an oriental, can beat.

I would like to endorse the
stand taken by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I think we should provide that the Chinaman should carry his certificate on his person and produce it on demand. The minister says truly enough that the production of it will not be any evidence that he has not obtained it by fraudulent means. That is true, but there is another phase of the matter. It is at least a certificate that he has one license, let him get it where he likes. It has this advantage: If you have a Chinese prisoner, and you ask him where his certificate is and he says it is at home and you let him go and get it, he will be sure to produce a certificate. But if you arrest him, you ask him to produce his certificate and he does not have it on him, that is evidence that he does not have one. If you let him go home where there are a couple of hundred Chinamen, he will certainly get a certificate, and there will be no way of discovering whether he did not simply borrow it. During the war every white man in Canada had to have a registration card and to produce it on request. No injustice was done and there was very little inconvenience. If provision were made in this legislation that a Chinaman must have his certificate on his person-and I certainly think such provision

Chinese Immigration.
should be made-that would be a means of detecting a great deal of this illicit work of shuffling around certificates, because a Chinaman might lend a man a certificate when he was going to court, but he would not give it to him if he himself had to carry it permanently on his person, as he himself might be caught without it and deported. I'think such a provision should be inserted in the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I might point out to my hon. friend that if this legislation were admitting any large number of Chinese, probably there would be some force in what he has just said. But the bill contemplates the admission of only the classes mentioned, and they will be very limited classes. They will be either of the student or the merchant class, and in all probability a very complete record will be kept of those individuals. There will, therefore, not be the same need for possession of a certificate on the person of an individual entering Canada under those classes as there would be if the persons being admitted were, for example, coolie labourers.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 18-Chinese to register within twelve months of date of the act!

I should like in this connection to remind the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart), or more properly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this would be a suitable occasion, when this registration is taking place, to give effect to the recommendation of the Duff Fisheries Commission of British Columbia last year that, as we had found so many cases of fraudulent naturalization papers, an opportunity should be taken to recall all those in British Columbia and revise them. The inference was that where it was found they were patently fraudulently obtained, for instance, if a man who was, say, twenty years old, had a certificate describing him as being fifty-five or sixty years of age, his certificate would be revoked. This would be a good occasion, when the registration by Chinamen is being made general, to have these papers revised as regards both Chinamen and Japanese. The recommendation of the Fisheries Commission in this regard was accepted by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All right.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On Section 19-Number of immigrants to be carried on each ship limited:
Is there any need of this clause? What is the idea of retaining it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is merely one other restriction on the number who can enter Canada..

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is this an old clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the former act the tonnage was fifty. It is now increased to two hundred and fifty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is built on the old section. Really, this seems a very absurd way of going at the subject. You might as well say that the number of immigrants must be regulated by the number of hairs on the captain's head.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On Section 20-Chinese persons not to leave ship without permit:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the explanation of this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This clause prohibits officers of any ship carrying Chinese to Canada permitting Chinese to leave the ship before all the formalities of the regulations have been observed. We have had some difficulty in connection with this in the past. This is to prevent Chinese sailors deserting at a Canadian port, and dishonest captains from permitting stowaways and others to leave the ship, and, in. this way, obtain surreptitious or illegal entry into Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On Section 21-Conductor to furnish list of Chinese persons carried:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the explanation of this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is to prevent conductors of railway trains allowing Chinese to obtain surreptitious entry into Canada by such trains.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are the provisions of clauses 20 and 21 in the general Immigration Act?	\

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not in such enlarged form. This is a much stiffer provision as regards both captains and railway conductors.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On Section 24-Re-entry:

As I read this clause, it constitutes really a further extension of this permission to return. If the minister will refer to sub-clause (3), there was a period about 1914 when conditions were pretty bad on the Pacific coast and permission was given
Chinese Immigration

to a large number of Chinese to return again to Canada within one or two years. That permission was extended by P.C. 697. If I recall the situation corectly, P.C. 697 has virtually expired but by this clause we are permitting return to Canada for the further period of a year from the coming into force of this legislation. I really do not think that should be done, and I will tell the minister once again why. What I have said before very largely applies to this. I doubt whether many who have not yet returned will return but substitutes will come who never were in the country before. I want to assure the minister that we are not overstating the case in constantly referring to this ability on the part of the Chinese to substitute one for another in these various matters. I am certain tl^at this will mean the entity into Canada of a considerable number of Chinese. A man will make a competency and go back without any intention of returning, but he will return in the person of another Chinaman; or he may go back and die, and there is always someone else to fill the gap. These are the things we are so bitterly opposed to. I see no reason whatever for this added permission and I would ask the minister, if it were not inconsistent with the legislation, and I do not think it is, to strike out subsection 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Subsection 3 provides for the return of Chinese who registered out between April first, 1914, and March 31st, 1919, and who, under the provisions of an order in council, P.C., 697, passed under the authority of the War Measures Act, were accorded the privilege of prolonging their return to Canada until one year after a proclamation had been published in the Canada Gazette declaring that a state of war no longer existed. No such proclamation has yet appeared in the Canada Gazette and it is possible it may never appear. There were at Vancouver registrations covering 572 Chinese who left during the period I have stated and who are still absent from Canada. The present section is to provide that they shall return within one year from the date of the coming into force of this act. They have under the order in council the extended time of one year after the publication in the Canada Gazette that a state of war no longer exists, but in view of the fact that such a declaration may not be published we are limiting the time of return to one year after the passing of this act.

What form did the termination of the war take? Our signing of the Peace Treaty ended the war, but I sup-

pose that when this terminology was used in the order in council it was prior to the conclusion of the war. I take it therefore that it was assumed that the publication of a declaration in the Canada Gazette would be the method of declaring the war at an end. Undoubtedly the intention of the order was to end the privilege with the termination of the war. What we are really doing by this legislation is extending the period for another year, and I think we ought to cancel now absolutely the privilege to any that have not returned to Canada because certainly they know perfectly well that they should have returned before now, and they are only taking advantage of a very strained interpretation of the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We will let this stand so that I may make further inquiry.
Section stands.
On section 2.5-Chinese sailors on Canadian vessels:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does this section admit Chinese assailors?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it provides for the outward registration of Chinese sailors employed on Canadian vessels operating between Canada and the United States. The Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia have ships operating between Vancouver and Seattle, making a round trip daily, and under the present act a Chinese sailor employed on such a ship must register daily. The cost of registration being a dollar it is proposed to change this and provide for the issuance of a certificate for a period of two years at a fee of $2.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would that apply to Chinese immigrants?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, merely to men sailing between ports.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Could not a Chinese immigrant come in and instead of landing on shore land in a boat and become a sailor and thereby become entitled to registration under this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would not be possible for him to do that because he would of necessity first - need to be in possession of a passport before he could make application for the certificate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 26-Arrest and deportation of any Chinese who has illegally entered or remained in Canada:

Chinese Immigration

Instead of "officer" in this section I think it should be "police officer". It is no use in the wilds of British Columbia to send two hundred miles to get a Chinese immigration officer; a police constable should be allowed to act under this section. The definition of officer in the interpretation clause is simply an immigration officer and such an officer would be found only in Vancouver, Victoria and possibly Nelson.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean that any police officer might demand the production of a certificate from a Chinese in Canada?

My hon. friend will have to pardon me for referring to our experiences so often, but we learn by experience. Only a few years ago quite a number of- Chinese or Japanese, I forgot which, landed on the west coast near my hon. friend's home. They did not touch a port of entry at all; they landed off the west coast of Vancouver Island, or Queen Charlotte Islands. There are constantly vessels running back and forth on the fishing grounds between different points, and as we are by this act restricting the ports of entry to Vancouver and Victoria, the only possible way of apprehending such people would be for a local officer to have some definite powers. If he were in the Queen Charlotte Islands it would take him in winter from two to three weeks to communicate with Vancouver.
Or Prince Rupert.
There would be no Chinese immigration agent there. It would be hopeless for any person to apprehend immigrants or control immigration of that kind under this clause. '

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would provincial police officers be satisfactory?
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I see a difficulty in keeping up a force of immigration officers.
Either provincial, municipal or Dominion police officers would do. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he keep an immigration officer at Prince Rupert.

This section would not give the policeman any drastic power because he can only arrest. Further down it is provided that the officer may detain an arrested person in custody and bring him before the nearest controller for examination. So that the man's rights are absolutely protected, and if a 149
police constable cannot be trusted to do this much he is not fit for the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not taking exception to the suggestion. I see the impossibility of patrolling a large area like British Columbia with immigration officials whose duty it would be to arrest people who obtain illegal entry.

I would suggest the words "police officer."
Section stands.
On section 27-Arrest and deportation of Chinese who ceases to belong to exempt or admissible classes:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Some exception has been taken to this section, and I do think that it is somewhat drastic.
Any person admitted as exempt from the tax under the provisions of the Chinese Immigration Act or any amendment thereto or under this act,-
It embodies the whole of it.
-and who at any time after admission ceases to belong to any of the exempt classes as defined by the Chinese Immigration Act or any amendment thereof or by this act,-
It seems to me this goes so far that if a Chinese merchant after being here for twenty years failed in his business and was obliged to become a labourer he would be subject to deportation.
That would be a very good thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of
Railways) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that the time within which the various provinces of Canada may earn and be paid the sums allotted to the said provinces under the provisions of The Canada Highways Act, chapter fifty-four of the statutes of 1919 be extended for a further period of two years.
Motion agreed to and House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Would the minister kindly give the reasons for this legislation, also a statement as to what has been expended and how much the various provinces have taken up of their respective quotas?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In 1919 an act was passed by the federal House providing for the payment to the various provinces of $20,000,000 to aid in the construction of roads. The grant was for a period of five years, which term expires in 1924. It will be necessary, however, for the provinces that are dependent on federal aid to know at this session what aid they can expect in arranging their plans for the years succeeding 1924. Several of the provinces have used up, or will have used up by the end of 1924, the various amounts to which they were entitled under the legislation of 1919. On the other hand, a number of them will not have expended the amounts to which they were entitled. The bill to be based on this resolution will extend the act of 1919 for two years to give those provinces that will not have used up the amount to which they were entitled by the end of 1924 an opportunity, during the next two years, to earn that amount. This seems to be an appropriate occasion to ask the government what decision has been reached with reference to the request of the provinces, made here within the last few weeks, to extend the principle of this legislation. speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
To put it briefly, this resolution is the answer of the government. After full deliberation considering the vast obligations of the Dominion it was thought advisable, and quite just and fair that this act should not be extended further than to allow those provinces which will not have been able to earn their apportionment by the expiration of 1924 to have ample opportunity to earn that portion of the appropriation. The deputation to which my hon. friend refers, I think, went away without any mistaken view as to what the attitude of the government was. The reply to their request was made by the Prime
Minister, who pointed out the fact, as I have stated, that our federal obligations were so great that the government thought it was time the provinces should look after the further development of good roads, and that the federal authorities should devote their attention and their expenditures to those things which necessarily come under federal authority. It was further pointed out that, while the war affected all parts of Canada, directly the expenses of the war fell upon the federal authorities, and the burden of taxation had risen to a point where the government believed it would not be justified at the present time in giving further aid to those things which are essentially provincial. That is the attitude of the government, as I stated before. We thought it would not be just to the provinces who had begun to develop a plan for good roads, believing they would have the entire amount of this appropriation at their disposal, to cut them off before they had their plans developed. This resolution is based on that principle, and it is proposed to extend the time so as to place all the provinces on an equal footing in regard to their ability and time to earn the amount of this appropriation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Whatever may be said for the government's decision, it cannot be said that it contributes to the relief of the tax-payer of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It does not add any more to it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There might be economies effected by the government that would, but anything effected by simply reducing what assistance has been given to the provinces merely adds to the tax burdens the provinces have to impose. It is a change in the taxcollecting agency, and that is all. A far better form of curtailment would be in those things that are federal, those things that have to do with the machinery and upkeep of government. This is merely a shifting of the instrument of collection.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: To the place where it belongs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
From the federal authority to the provincial. Constitutionally the obligation of roadmaking and upkeep of roads is of course provincial, that cannot be disputed, but of course the Dominion has very frequently assisted the provinces in more than one of the functions the provinces carry on. For instance, we are making grants for agricultural education. We are conducting agricultural services. These are fundamentally provincial. But that is not the point I rose to
Canada Highways Act

emphasize, which was that this proposition may take a burden off the government, but it does not take any burden off the people. It may make the estimates of this government that much less, but it is not by economizing that the government brings it about. It is merely bj>- shifting to the provinces the load that, for general purposes and in the public interests, the federal government assumed in 1919.
This policy has resulted undoubtedly in a stimulus being given to road building in this country. We were very far behind the United States, and I do not doubt for a moment but that this country is suffering now, in comparison with the United States, in the retention of its population, in the attraction of new population, in business activities, from many reasons, one of which is the superiority of transit on the roads in that country. In Canada we are far behind them indeed, and the object of the legislation was to give such an impetus to them, and to have such a momentum aroused, that the provinces would go on and continue the work of roadmaking on a permanent interprovincial and lasting basis. It has had that effect to a degree. It has had it to a very considerable degree. I apprehend that the breaking of it off will result in the patch-work character of roads in Canada. I knew the time would likely come sooner or later when the matter would be again left to the provinces, but I fear the high cost of roadmaking of recent years-that is the extent to which that high cost was unexpected and was unprovided for-will all be reflected in a broken patch-work system of roads. We shall find the country with pieces of road here and pieces there, but nothing linked up. That will likely be one of the results; but whether or not it is justified, I want only to emphasize that it is not brought about by any economy of administration, it is simply shoving back on the provinces a load that in other days we undertook to carry.

It seems to me, on this question of road building, after all the people pay. It does not matter whether it is the Dominion government or the provincial government, the money comes from the people. In connection with municipal affairs, I have had some little experience in bulding roads, and I do not know that government aid is just the best thing in some circumstances. I believe Manitoba would to-day be in a better position if it had a good many roads yet to build that it has already built, and built at a time when wages were high and expenses of every kind 
enormous. With the fillip that it got from advances from the Dominion government and advances from the provincial government, the idea was: Go on and build the roads; go after all those grants, and, of course, in that way the province ran into pretty large expenses and debts. I am a believer in good roads. The measure of a country's civilization is known by the way in which it goes about road building. At the same time I want to point out the fact that nearly all the big road building that has been done in the Dominion of Canada has been done at the most expensive time when it could possibly have been done, when help was scarce and when it cost an enormous amount of money to get the work done. In the municipality in which I was interested, we used to get the work done for 20 to 25 cents a yard; whereas during the time the great bulk of the road building was done, this cost 40 to 45 cents a yard. This shows the enormous cost of carrying on road building. The government in this case is neither to be praised nor to be blamed. I think about the right thing to do is to drop this policy in the meantime.

I think the government is to be congratulated on bringing to an end on fair terms a system whereby one power supplies the money and another power spends it. That system is essentially unwise. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) seems in a half-hearted sort of way to blame the government for its declared intention of bringing this system to an end. In this country we have more or less gone transportation mad. We have applied to transportation systems, whether railway, canal or otherwise, far more of the public revenue than it was wise to do. I am thoroughly of opinion that we shall put the finances of this country on a sound basis if we adhere, more largely in the future than we have done in the past, to the principle which forces the government that is spending the money to the unpleasant task of raising the money. I cannot help congratulating the government on its declared intention, as I understand it, of' bringing this system to an end. This legislation of 1919 may have had a good effect. It may, however, have had the effect of encouraging provinces to embark in schemes of expenditure which they did not want, and which it was unwise for them to embark upon. The question of roads is, in its primary aspect, the question of a good road to market, to church and to the station, and a great deal of our expenditure on great-trunk highways which serve largely as plea-

Canada Highways Act
sure roads for pleasure travel is in my humble opinion, an extravagance of which a country in our financial condition should make the most sparing use.
How much remains to be drawn for New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: About $300,000. It is estimated that it will be expended fully by the end of 1924.

No further grant is proposed to provinces which will have earned their proportion of the appropriation of $20,000,000.

I do not agree with the stand taken by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and other hon. gentlemen, that the Dominion should not do anything further to assist in building good roads. In British Columbia particularly there are reasons why we should receive assistance. The country there is of such a nature that road-building is very difficult and very expensive. I do not know that there have been any allegations as to the misapplication of funds or the throwing away of money in connection with the building of roads in the province. If there has been anything wrong in that connection, then of course the Liberal government must be responsible for it, because we have had a Liberal government there all that time. But I suggest that the money which has been spent, although it may have been spent in an extravagant way, has possibly been spent to advantage; that is to say, we have received benefits from the work which has been done. In British Columbia some very good roads have been built which are not in all respects of a provincial character. For instance, the Pacific highway which connects with a road from Vancouver to San Diego in southern California, a distance of some two thousand miles, is one of such roads. I think the construction of that road is going to be a good thing for British Columbia and consequently for Canada. It is going to bring in a great many motorists who are all going to spend money and some of whom will undoubtedly remain in the country. The construction of that road I believe was a splendid thing for Canada.
Another road is required and that is across British Columbia from the east to the west. In my opinion the rest of Canada is interested in that road to a certain extent. Certainly the mountainous scenery of British Columbia is unsurpassed in the world and is a great asset to Canada as a whole. It seems to me a matter for regret that in order to get from British Columbia to the province of Alberta it is necessary for us to go through the United States if we wish to travel by motor. It would be a good thing if a road
Canada Highways Act

could be built across British Columbia, and I think that the Dominion should do something to assist in the construction of such a road. The same principle would apply to other provinces. I am firmly convinced that money spent either by the Dominion or by the provinces in the construction of good roads is as well expended as any money can be. In this country we are not as far advanced in this respect as they are in other places, and this government should consider extending the programme of assistance federally to the provinces for the building of roads.
